lead: A cutting tool must stay harder than the work metal while the edge is hot. Carbon steel loses hardness first; high-speed steel holds it further; carbide, ceramic, CBN and diamond hold it further still. The tool material sets the safe cutting speed. A cutting fluid carries heat away, lowers friction, flushes chips and guards against corrosion. Together they decide whether a lathe or milling job runs smoothly or fails by rapid wear.
prereq: You need: 5.3 tool geometry and tool signature, because rake angle and nose radius change how a tool material performs.

blocks.text: The cutting edge sees stress, abrasion and high temperature together. The key property is hot hardness: the hardness a material keeps at the temperature of the cutting zone. A material with low hot hardness softens, rubs and wears quickly. Toughness resists chipping under interrupted cuts. Wear resistance resists flank and crater wear. Cost decides what a shop can use every day.

items: Carbon tool steel: 0.6–1.3% carbon, cheap and sharp, but it loses its temper and softens above roughly 200–250 °C, so it is limited to hand tools and low cutting speeds.
High-speed steel (HSS): 18-4-1 means 18% tungsten, 4% chromium, 1% vanadium and about 0.7% carbon by mass. It is tough and holds hardness to about 600 °C. Used for drills, taps, hobs and form tools.
Cemented carbide: tungsten carbide (WC) grains held in cobalt (Co) binder. Very hard and wear resistant, but brittle. It is used as clamped inserts; grades change with cobalt content.

Coated carbide: a thin layer of TiN, TiC or Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> on a carbide insert. The coating lowers friction and slows crater wear, so the insert runs at higher speed. Coated and uncoated grades are not interchangeable.
Cermet: ceramic particles in a metal binder. It sits between carbide and ceramic, gives good finish on steel, and is less tough than carbide.

Ceramic, CBN and diamond: ceramic (alumina or silicon nitride) is chemically stable and very hard but brittle. Cubic boron nitride (CBN) cuts hardened steel and cast iron. Diamond is hardest and is used on aluminium, copper, glass and composites, never on steel because carbon diffuses into iron.

blocks.text: Use the table to compare, not to rank every grade. A tough HSS drill survives shock that would chip a ceramic insert.

sections.h3: Cutting fluids: four jobs, four families

blocks.text: A cutting fluid does four jobs: it cools the tool and work, lubricates the sliding chip on the rake face, flushes chips away, and protects the machine from corrosion. Cooling matters most at high speed, where most heat enters the chip and tool. Lubrication matters most at low speed, where friction on the rake face is large.

items: Straight oil: neat mineral or fatty oil. Good lubrication, poor cooling, and it can smoke. Used for low-speed severe work and some non-ferrous metals.
Soluble oil: oil dispersed in water. Good cooling with some lubrication. The common general-purpose fluid for turning, milling and drilling.
Semi-synthetic: a water-mixed fluid with less oil and more chemical additives. It balances cooling, lubrication and cleanliness.
Synthetic: no mineral oil; water with chemical additives. Best cooling and corrosion control, often used in grinding and high-speed machining.

blocks.text: Selection follows the job. Water-based fluid where heat is the problem; neat oil where friction is the problem. Magnesium is unsafe with water because it can react and burn; aluminium needs an inhibitor to stop staining. Cast iron can be cut dry because graphite in the chip helps lubrication.

Application methods are flooding, mist and minimum quantity lubrication (MQL). Flooding sends a continuous stream at the cutting zone and is the shop default. Mist carries fine fluid droplets in an air stream; the droplets evaporate at the cutting zone, so it cools reasonably well but lubricates poorly, and the airborne droplets are a health risk that needs extraction and PPE. MQL sends a small, metered oil flow carried in an air jet straight to the cutting zone. It replaces the flood stream, cuts fluid waste and disposal cost, and suits high-speed cuts in a rigid machine where the chips carry most of the heat. See 5.5 for how heat turns into wear.

sections.h3: Matching tool and fluid to speed

blocks.text: The tool material sets a speed limit. Carbon steel runs slowly. HSS runs faster and survives shock. Uncoated carbide runs faster still on steady cuts. Coated carbide adds a thermal barrier and lower friction, so it runs faster again. Ceramic, CBN and diamond run at the top end, but they are brittle and need rigid machines.

The fluid must match that choice. At low speed with HSS, a neat oil or rich soluble oil gives lubrication. At high speed with coated carbide, a water-based flood carries heat away. In a rigid CNC cell, MQL may replace flood for a controlled cut.

Never treat the fluid as a coolant only. It also controls friction, chip clearing and rust. A wrong fluid can stain aluminium, crack a carbide insert by thermal shock, or create a fire risk with magnesium. The correct pair of tool and fluid lowers temperature, slows wear and holds surface finish.

examples.question: An 18-4-1 high-speed steel contains 18% tungsten, 4% chromium, 1% vanadium and 0.7% carbon by mass. A tool blank has mass 250 g. Find the mass of tungsten, chromium, vanadium and carbon in the blank.
examples.answer: The 250 g blank contains 45 g tungsten, 10 g chromium, 2.5 g vanadium and 1.75 g carbon.
examples.check:
w = 0.18 * 250
cr = 0.04 * 250
v = 0.01 * 250
c = 0.007 * 250
print(w)
print(cr)
print(v)
print(c)

traps: Carbide is not a single material. WC-Co grades change with cobalt content and grain size, and coated carbide is a different grade from uncoated carbide.

18-4-1 gives the composition by mass: 18% tungsten, 4% chromium and 1% vanadium. The remaining mass is mostly iron (about 76%) plus about 0.7% carbon. Do not read the three numbers as grams, kilograms or ratio units; they are mass percentages, so a 250 g blank holds 45 g tungsten, not 18 g.
Water-mixed fluid is not universal. Magnesium can react with water and burn; aluminium needs a corrosion inhibitor; some low-speed severe cuts need neat oil.
Diamond does not cut every metal. Carbon diffuses into iron at cutting temperature, so diamond is not used on steel.
Higher cost does not always mean a better tool. A brittle ceramic insert can fail on an interrupted cut where tough HSS survives.

quiz.q: Name four functions of a cutting fluid.
quiz.a: Cooling the tool and work, lubricating the chip on the rake face, flushing chips away, and protecting against corrosion.

quiz.q: Why does carbon tool steel fail at high cutting speed?
quiz.a: Carbon steel has low hot hardness. At high speed the cutting zone becomes hot, the edge softens, and it wears or deforms quickly.

quiz.q: A 400 g HSS blank contains 18% tungsten by mass. Find the mass of tungsten.
A shop uses water-soluble cutting fluid on magnesium. Why is this unsafe?
quiz.a: Magnesium can react with water to produce hydrogen and heat, creating a fire or explosion risk. Neat oil or dry cutting is used instead.

quiz.q: Why is diamond not used to cut steel?
quiz.a: At cutting temperature carbon from diamond diffuses into iron, so the diamond edge wears chemically very fast. Diamond is used on aluminium, copper, glass and composites instead.

quiz.q: Choose a tool material for turning hardened steel at high speed: HSS, uncoated carbide or CBN. Give one reason.
quiz.a: CBN. It keeps hardness and wear resistance at high temperature on hardened steel, where HSS softens and carbide wears too fast.

quiz.q: A coated carbide insert lasts longer than an uncoated insert at the same cutting speed. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: The coating lowers friction on the rake face, reducing heat and crater wear. It also acts as a thermal barrier, so the carbide substrate stays cooler and retains hardness.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coated tools now use multilayer PVD and CVD stacks, and MQL or cryogenic cooling is used in production to cut fluid waste. Search for 'tool coating architecture', 'minimum quantity lubrication machining' and 'cryogenic turning'. Additive-made cooling channels inside inserts are an active research area.
